title: The Role of Cardiac Troponin and Other Emerging Biomarkers Among Athletes and Beyond: Underlying Mechanisms, Differential Diagnosis, and Guide for Interpretation
content: Cardiovascular (CV) disease remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, highlighting the necessity of understanding its underlying molecular and pathophysiological pathways. Conversely, physical activity (PA) and exercise are key strategies in reducing CV event risk. Detecting latent CV conditions in apparently healthy individuals, such as athletes, presents a unique challenge. Early identification and treatment of CV disorders are vital for long-term health and patient survival. Thus, there is a pressing need to identify and implement more sensitive and specific biomarkers for CV disorders in clinical practice. Similarly, research continues to explore reliable biomarkers for evaluating the health of athletes and the effectiveness of physical exercise. Cardiac troponin is currently the most commonly used biomarker for assessing CV changes in both athletes and the general population. However, there remains considerable debate surrounding the mechanisms underlying exercise-induced troponin elevations and its release in non-ischemic contexts. This has led to a new research focus on biomarkers, such as exosomes and cytokines, which may provide deeper insights. This review aims to summarize current research on cytokines and exosomes, their physiological roles, and their relevance in various CV conditions, especially in athletes. Special attention is given to underlying mechanisms, potential as biomarkers, and future perspectives. Furthermore, we review current evidence on troponin release in non-ischemic conditions, post-strenuous exercise, and the complex biological pathways that influence its detection.
